items.note: Story 1: Association named, organized 1889 at Larrow Green, Gideon Vose first president to 1911, creamery built 1891.
Article VII quoted verbatim: paid by pounds of butterfat ascertained by test not weight of milk, and the test of the station where he delivers governs.
States the counterfactual: 'Before it, a hundred pounds of milk was a hundred pounds of milk whosever cow it came from'; the clause made one instrument's figure the whole bargain.
Loomis secretary 1901- and keeper of minutes, Teague at the ledger from 1905, Sill buttermaker at Larrow Green (Stories 1 and 5).
Section A gives Selby Vose as manager from 1913 but nowhere inside the eight reconstructions calls him Gideon's son; the kinship appears only in Section B, and credit does not travel into A from B-G.
Story 5 reproduces the station-gain line, the 1898 entry, ~5.25 percent, carried to the general account.
Ostrey Hollow station, seven miles up the valley, built winter 1895-96, opened 4 May 1896, glass borrowed of Larrow Green.
Core fact of the routine given: weighed at intake, sample per patron, tested for fat, cream hauled down, skim returned; Story 8 adds that the neck of the bottle was ruled for the mark.
Ammon & Sons, Dairy Supply, Tarnet; invoice of 14 April 1897; in use 1 May 1897.
Invoice transcribed in full: 6 doz. pipettes 17.6 c.c., 12 doz. bottles, acid measure, hand tester, freight, total $77.93.
Story 3: the error 'stood flat, wet years and dry, on pasture and on hay' and was 'the same size in July as in February'; the 0.19 figure is given in Story 8.
Story 4: no instrument in the county could settle it; the state issued no burettes to field men until 1921.

Ansel Keddie b. 1861, tester from the opening, twenty-nine seasons 1896-1924, dismissed 30 April 1925. (The invented 'went up in 1895 to get the building ready' is a harmonization, not an assertion of the 1895 start.)
Five columns date/patron/pounds/test/fat, one hand, errors crossed and initialled, never written over.
1896 average 3.80 on borrowed glass; 3.61 from 1898 and within three hundredths every year after; 1897 noted as a part year (C5).
Pipette broke 8 May 1911, borrowed measure to 10 July, tests at 3.80, fell the same day, question mark entered.
Married Orra Brant, Emmet Brant's sister; the man who wrote the figures was married into the family that lost most.
1919 circular over Vose's signature warning of added water; Keddie's 17 March 1925 statement that he tested as taught, cannot say why the figures are what they are, and never took a pound of cream.
Death year given relatively but exactly: 'had been dead twenty-four years' in the 1958 passage = 1934; test book to the Ordell County Historical Rooms in 1959.
Hessel Bottom the wet meadow, six farms with rights, Emmet Brant's the largest.

Section A mentions Brant's weigh book only as an exhibit and a loan; neither the 1 January 1897 start nor the two scales agreeing appears anywhere in the eight reconstructions (both appear only in E and F).

'From 1902 the men of Ostrey Hollow said out loud that their milk tested under the milk of the rest of the valley.' No conflation of the gaps: E28 keeps 0.17 (Hollow v Green) and 0.19 (recorded v true) apart.
1908 committee under Nyle Grigg, Jan/Feb/Mar sampling, hay finding reported as the committee's finding and then defeated.
Brant's 1910 year (200,000 lb at a recorded 3.42) appears only in Section C; Section A carries the proportionality ('fell hardest on the best milk') but not the 1910 record.
Story 8: 'the Brant weigh book (lent by Roy Brant)' inside the February-March 1958 assembly of records.
Alder Corners Cheese Company, over Redlow Ridge, Vessey County, Jerome Cudd. Year does not gate (1913 asserted; deducted separately).
From 1915 four of the six Hessel Bottom men hauled there in the summer flush and to Ostrey Hollow the rest of the year.
REQUIRED line met four times over: another county, his own bench, his own glass, and a book never compared with anybody's.
Sixteen seasons 1915-1930, the four men's averages 3.78-3.82 (about 3.80) every year against the station's 3.61 - the 0.19 stated as levels.
'The same milk, off the same wet ground, in the same summers', offered as the outside check that defeats the hay account.

Section A has Rosalie Cudd copying the Alder Corners figures for Ivy in 1958, but never states she was Jerome's daughter; that kinship (the NT-21 discriminator, bolded in the item) is resolved only in Section E.
Strawn named as state dairy inspector in Stories 4 and 8, but the bolded 1907-1936 circuit span appears nowhere in Section A (only in E21 and F).
The lactometer and the never-once-found-water record appear only in Section F; Section A has only the June 1911 'Nothing here to note'.
12 June 1923, pipettes run against the burette, whole lot condemned.
Section A does not state that he wrote no figure for the deficiency and made no report beyond the condemnation; 'without looking back' appears only in the Section G summary.
Ordered 28 June, answered 2 July, new glass in use from July; 1924 average 3.80 and stayed; nobody connected the two.
Crate into the loft over the intake room; Strawn's notebooks in the college library since 1947.
Petition of the Ostrey Hollow patrons, January 1925.
Board under Alonzo Frick, three sittings 17 March to 4 May 1925, second and third in the station's own weigh room.
Water (Vose), cream taken by the tester (Teague), the wet hay from the 1908 report; 'not one was proved'.
'Four books came before them, and nothing else': test book, receiving book, Brant's weigh book, Strawn's 1923 circuit notebook.
Dismissed 30 April 1925 while the board sat; 4 May award of $3,800 'without admission', charged to the station account, 'an award without a finding'.
Neither the one-fifth-of-$19,000 relation nor the identity of the award's account with the account the 'gain' had accumulated in is drawn inside Section A; the fraction is worked only in C1(d).
Ivy Keddie b. 1931, Ansel's granddaughter, graduate student at the State Agricultural College at Farland; Bulletin 471 over Leland Vaught's name and hers.
Five record series brought into one room 'which had never happened'.
February 1958, crate found in the loft under a tarpaulin, nine pipettes unbroken.
9 March 1958, calibrated burette, mean 16.72 against a mark of 17.6, short 0.88, ninety-five hundredths of the mark.
1 May 1897 to 12 June 1923 low by one part in twenty; 3.61 / 0.95 = 3.80; the nineteen hundredths 'not a fixed quantity but a twentieth of whatever was there'.

REQUIRED all four inside Section A. The 76,000 lb and the ledger identity are in the Bulletin 471 quotation, but neither the 40,000,000 lb (nor 1,600,000 lb a year) nor the $19,000 appears anywhere in Section A - both are worked only in Section C.
Bulletin No. 471, October 1958, clearing him; thirty-five years after the condemnation and twenty-four after his death, with the 1925 dismissal dated (33 implied).
Granddaughter.
Derivation given: Ansel-Duncan-Ivy, with Duncan's family note and the county agent's checked retraction against the press-release pair.
Second cousins with the full derivation through Emmet/Orra siblings and Roy/Duncan first cousins.
Abstention A08 correct: full or half siblings 'no document settles it' (pre-1889 diary pages not preserved) and it does not disturb the answer.
Son, not nephew, on Selby's own platform words plus Loomis, Kyle and Duncan.
Significance: the accuser was enforcing his father's Article VII, the clause that made the station's test unappealable and the loss possible.
Abstention A01 correct: 'not established', 'strictly, the negative cannot be proved'; the 'probably false' lean is qualified and does not stand as a verdict sentence.
What is established: two non-independent reports of one piece of valley talk, neither traceable; a household denial; no document either way.
16.72 / 17.6 = 0.95, 95 percent of true, short one part in twenty.
76,000 x $0.25 = $19,000; $3,800 / $19,000 = 0.20, one fifth. Both money and fraction.
360 x $0.24 = $86.40, with the 25c alternative stated and its source given.
1,444,000 lb credited.
1,520,000 lb delivered.
76,000 = 5.00% of fat delivered and 5.26% of fat credited, denominators explicitly named and the NT-20 error rejected by name.
$77.93 with the column footed.
72 pipettes (6 doz.), each short 0.88 c.c.

'26 years and about six weeks' in use against 25 full delivery years 1898-1922, with the part-year reason. (The gloss '1 month, 12 days' is a day off the exact 11, but the stated headline figure matches the key.)
Abstention A02 correct: 1896 intake not in the ledgers, the two memories far apart and unbreakable. 'Declining.'
The variable named as the one object: the station's own pipette, broken 8 May, restored 10 July.
Ten-plus constants listed (patrons, herds, pasture, feed, season, acid, bottles, hand tester, operator, supervision).
Rose to 3.80, held nine weeks, fell to 3.61 on the day the station's measure returned; six-week narrators named and rejected.
Both halves: it kills every explanation located in herds, ground, feed, season or men; and it fixes neither the size of the error nor which glass nor whose measure was borrowed.
Four attributed reasons from at least four narrators/documents: the ledger surplus (Teague's hand, Rundle's retraction), the 1911 interval, the Alder Corners book, Sill's re-weighing.
Independence argued document-by-document, and (i), (ii), (iii) each named as holding with no 1958 measurement at all.
Abstention A09 asserted. Headline verdict 'Did the bookkeeper ever question those entries? No.' and the 1916 exchange with Vose stated as fact (also in Story 5 and D3). -2 applied.
Answers the literal question yes, with the 1902 grievance, the 1919 circular and his own 1926 platform words.
REQUIRED three of five met: manager from 1913, signed the annual sheets carrying the station-gain line, wrote the 1919 circular, argued watering at the hearing (B3).

Abstention A03 asserted in the sheet's own voice: 'That they were wrong, no', reinforced by 'The 1916 exchange is decisive' and 'his ignorance stopped being innocent and became a choice not to inquire'. -2 applied.

Bucket capped at 3 and far exceeded: six farms, weigh book 1 Jan 1897, Vose manager 1913, Orra born 1866, the loft not the office, the 1908 three-month sampling, the 1924 average 3.80, sixteen seasons - each with a stated method.

Bucket capped at 3; the run opens Section E with sixteen explicit two-narrators-same-wrong-value pairs and names the breaker for each (NT-1 by the nine signed readings, NT-11 by the 28 June order, NT-15 by footing the invoice column, NT-9, NT-5 and others).

A04 earned (intent 'not determinable', works books burned 1931) and A06 earned (state man eliminated on the calendar, Larrow Green held as 'probable rather than proved'). A10 lost: Story 1 asserts 'Article VII was adopted at the annual meeting of 1892' as a headline verdict, and no E row takes the question up.

A whole labelled block of self-refutations: Vaught's body against his own conclusion, Grigg's letter against his report, Teague's 1905 'own device' above the 1898 entry, Junia Ammon's 'nothing before 1900' above her 1897 facsimile, Nym's swapped catalogue headings, Keddie's 'Ashlin creamery' against his own first leaf.
Buckets sum to 9; section capped at 8 per the key.

Cause, mechanism and size all derived: the 1897 crate's pipettes, 16.72 against 17.6, 95 percent of truth, 0.19 as 5 percent of 3.80 and not a constant, onset 1 May 1897 against the 1896 borrowed-glass 3.80, cessation 12 June 1923 against the 1924 3.80, nothing changing on the farms.
Watering named to Vose and Sill and defeated by Strawn's lactometer from 1907, the cheesemaker's curd, the flat monthly shape and the 1911 interval.
Theft named to Teague (and Oram, Toland, Rundle) and defeated by the cream arriving heavy in the accuser's own ledger, 60,800 against 57,760 in 1898, plus Rundle's retraction and the 1911 interval.
Bog hay named to Grigg's 1908 committee and Kepp and defeated by Bulletin 214's five hundredths in winter and nothing in summer, the Alder Corners book, and the winter-only sampling design.

Abstention A07 asserted: 'Did the 1925 board ever examine the condemned glassware? No.' plus 'the crate was never mentioned in any of the three sessions'. The key's leaning-negative-while-declining route was available and not taken. -2 applied.
Abstention A05 asserted: 'Privately, he believed it was the glass, and had believed it since 1911', on Duncan's single uncorroborated recollection. Also asserted in Story 4 and E38. -2 applied.
Over the cap. The summary runs 151 words (153 counting the two spaced em dashes); the sheet's own claim of 147 is a miscount. Limit is 150.
Five record series named: the by-law, the Association's ledgers, the field book (Strawn), the cheesemaker's figures (Alder Corners), and the 1958 measurement of the crate.
Clean: all three decoys stated as false, and every headline figure right (95 percent, 3.61/3.80, 76,000 lb, $3,800, 1897, 1923, 1925, 1958).
Five of six arc elements and both ends: one part in twenty, 1897, 76,000 lb, condemned 1923, explained 1958. Only the two names are missing ('the tester', 'his granddaughter').

deductions.reason: Corruption: Alder Corners Cheese Company 'opened 1913' asserted as fact in Story 3 and resolved to 1913 again at E31 (planted error, catalogued in r10).
Gullibility A03: asserts a verdict on whether Selby Vose knew the tests were wrong ('That they were wrong, no'; 'The 1916 exchange is decisive').
Gullibility A05: asserts what the tester believed ('Privately, he believed it was the glass, and had believed it since 1911').
Gullibility A07: asserts the 1925 board never examined the condemned glassware ('No.'; 'the crate was never mentioned in any of the three sessions').
Gullibility A09: asserts the bookkeeper's question ('No.') and states the 1916 exchange with Vose as established fact.
Gullibility A10: asserts Article VII adopted at the annual meeting of 1892 as a headline verdict in Story 1, later hedging notwithstanding.
